question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fraction ε of individuals are fully protected (hazard 0) while the rest have no protection (hazard λ, same as unvaccinated). This means the per-exposure VE equals ε. The observed hazard among the vaccinated is time-varying because the unprotected subgroup is depleted faster than the unvaccinated population. Consequently, the person-time-weighted IRR is < 1-ε, so 1-IRR > ε. Thus 1-IRR overestimates per-exposure VE (choice A).

(The initial instantaneous IRR equals 1-ε, but any realistic follow-up period produces a downward bias in the average IRR.)

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fraction \(v\) of recipients are fully protected (infection probability 0 per exposure) while the remainder experience the same per-exposure risk \(p\) as unvaccinated individuals. The group-average per-exposure efficacy is therefore exactly \(v\). Under a constant hazard (or Poisson exposure) model the vaccinated incidence rate is simply \((1-v)\) times the unvaccinated rate, so \(1-\text{IRR}=v\). Hence the incidence-rate-ratio estimator recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias. 

C. correctly estimate

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns an all-or-nothing vaccine (a random fraction p of recipients are fully protected; the remainder receive zero protection). Per-exposure VE in this model is exactly p.  

Because only the unprotected fraction (1-p) ever contributes events, the incidence rate in the vaccinated arm equals (1-p) times the incidence rate in the unvaccinated arm at every instant. Consequently the incidence-rate ratio remains constantly equal to 1-p and 1-IRR recovers p without bias. (The same algebra shows the ratio is also constant, and unbiased, for a leaky vaccine; the distinction between the two vaccine actions appears only when cumulative incidence or time-varying hazards are examined.)  

Thus 1-IRR correctly estimates per-exposure VE.  

Final answer: C

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, the 1-incidence rate ratio will underestimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. The incidence rate ratio aggregates events across the full follow-up period and therefore mixes protected and unprotected individuals in a way that attenuates the apparent effect relative to the sharp, binary protection that occurs on each individual exposure. Because the measure is not conditioned on the exact number of exposures per person, the resulting efficacy estimate ends up lower than the true per-exposure protection that would be observed if exposure counts were explicitly accounted for. This underestimation is a direct consequence of the all-or-nothing mechanism interacting with the aggregate nature of the incidence rate.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a proportion p of recipients become completely immune while the remainder are unaffected. This directly scales the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated group by exactly (1-p) relative to the unvaccinated group, so the incidence rate ratio equals 1-p. Consequently 1-IRR recovers p exactly, which is the per-exposure (or individual) efficacy parameter in the all-or-nothing model. (By contrast, the same estimator would be biased for a leaky vaccine.) Thus the correct choice is C.

(The question supplies no numerical values or exposure schedules that would alter the equality, reinforcing that the estimator is unbiased.)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine (complete protection in a fraction of individuals, none in the rest), the observed hazards satisfy hazard_vax = (1 - p) * hazard_unvax at every instant. Thus IRR is constantly equal to 1 - p, so 1 - IRR recovers p exactly—the per-exposure efficacy averaged across individuals. (Depletion of susceptibles does not bias the ratio because only the unprotected fraction in the vaccinated arm is ever at risk.) Hence the answer is C.

(The question wording distinguishes “per-exposure” from “all-or-nothing,” but the algebra shows they coincide here.)

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The incidence rate ratio (IRR) measures the ratio of new infections per unit of person-time between vaccinated and unvaccinated cohorts under a constant force of infection. For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fixed fraction \(\varepsilon\) of recipients receive complete (sterilizing) protection while the remainder receive none. Consequently the vaccinated cohort always contains exactly the fraction \((1-\varepsilon)\) susceptibles; each of those susceptibles experiences the identical per-exposure hazard as unvaccinated individuals.  

Because the proportion of susceptibles remains constant over time and the exposure intensity is the same in both arms, the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is exactly \((1-\varepsilon)\) times the incidence rate in the unvaccinated arm at every instant. Therefore IRR \(= 1-\varepsilon\) throughout follow-up, and \(1-\)IRR recovers \(\varepsilon\) without bias. In short, the per-exposure protection conferred by the all-or-nothing mechanism is correctly estimated by \(1-\)IRR.  

This equality does not hold for cumulative incidence ratios (which become time-dependent) or for leaky vaccines under certain depletion regimes, but the question asks specifically about the incidence-rate measure under the all-or-nothing model.  

Final answer: C. correctly estimate

PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a proportion p of individuals are fully protected (100% per-exposure efficacy) while the remainder have 0% protection. This produces a constant hazard ratio of exactly (1-p) between groups, regardless of exposure frequency or depletion of susceptibles. Therefore 1-IRR recovers p exactly, which is also the average per-exposure efficacy. (By contrast, risk ratios can diverge from per-exposure efficacy under leaky models, but the question specifies IRR.)

C. correctly estimate

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns an all-or-nothing vaccine (fraction \(p\) of recipients fully protected with per-exposure susceptibility = 0; fraction \(1-p\) completely unaffected with per-exposure susceptibility = 1). The population-average per-exposure VE is therefore exactly \(p\).

Under a constant force of infection \(\lambda\), the incidence rate (cases per person-time) among the unvaccinated equals \(\lambda\) exactly. Among the vaccinated the observed IRR equals
\[
(1-p)\frac{\text{PT}_\text{unvax}}{pT+(1-p)\text{PT}_\text{unvax}},
\]
where \(\text{PT}_\text{unvax}<T\). This expression is strictly less than \(1-p\), so
\[
1-\text{IRR}>p.
\]
Hence the incidence-rate-ratio estimator systematically overestimates the per-exposure VE. The correct choice is therefore A.

(The same algebra shows the bias grows with follow-up time \(T\), as protected individuals contribute ever more “empty” person-time.)

Final answer: A. overestimate

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the protection is effectively a step function (full immunity or none), so the observed incidence rates reflect the fraction of fully protected individuals plus the exposure intensity in the unprotected fraction. The 1-IRR therefore mixes the binary protection status with the average number of exposures per person; because incidence accumulates over multiple exposures in the susceptible group, the ratio ends up smaller than the true per-exposure reduction that would be seen in a single-exposure setting. Hence the incidence-based estimate understates the underlying per-exposure efficacy.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine I believe the 1-incidence rate ratio will underestimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy. The reason is that an all-or-nothing mechanism immediately removes a fixed fraction of vaccinated individuals from the risk set entirely; the remaining incidence therefore reflects only the unprotected subgroup. Because the rate ratio is computed over the whole vaccinated cohort (including those who contribute zero events), the observed ratio ends up smaller than the true per-exposure protection that would be measured in a setting where every exposure is independent. Hence 1-IRR lies below the per-exposure value.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns standard definitions from vaccine epidemiology (e.g., Halloran et al.). An all-or-nothing vaccine confers complete protection to a fraction \(v\) of recipients and zero protection to the remainder.  

Under this model the vaccinated cohort therefore contains only a fraction \((1-v)\) of susceptibles. Because those susceptibles experience exactly the same per-exposure hazard as unvaccinated individuals, the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is exactly \((1-v)\) times the incidence rate in the unvaccinated arm at every moment. Consequently the incidence-rate ratio equals \(1-v\) exactly, and \(1-\)IRR recovers \(v\) without bias.  

Here \(v\) is also the average per-exposure efficacy (complete protection for proportion \(v\), none for \(1-v\)), so the estimator is unbiased. (Contrast with a leaky vaccine, where the same estimator is biased.)  

Thus the correct choice is C.  

(The conclusion follows directly from the constant hazard ratio implied by the all-or-nothing assumption; no simulation or external data are required.)

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine, a fixed fraction \(p\) of individuals receive complete protection (per-exposure efficacy = 1) while the remainder receive none (per-exposure efficacy = 0). The average per-exposure efficacy is therefore exactly \(p\).

Under a standard individual-level hazard model the force of infection acting on every susceptible person is identical in the vaccinated and unvaccinated arms. Consequently the proportion of the vaccinated cohort that remains susceptible is constantly scaled by the factor \((1-p)\). The observed incidence rate is therefore also constantly scaled by \((1-p)\), so the incidence-rate ratio equals \(1-p\) at every instant. Hence \(1-\text{IRR}\) recovers \(p\) exactly and does not over- or underestimate the per-exposure efficacy.

(The same constancy holds for a leaky vaccine, but that is outside the scope of the present question.)

Final answer: C. correctly estimate

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: For an all-or-nothing vaccine a fixed fraction p of recipients are fully protected (per-exposure susceptibility reduced by 100 %) while the remaining 1-p receive zero protection. Under a constant hazard (or fixed number of exposures) the observed incidence rate in the vaccinated arm is therefore exactly (1-p) times the rate in the unvaccinated arm. Consequently IRR = 1-p and 1-IRR recovers p, which is the average per-exposure efficacy. The estimator is therefore unbiased. (By contrast, the same 1-IRR applied to a leaky vaccine underestimates the constant per-exposure efficacy.)

C. correctly estimate

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The question concerns how incidence rate ratio (IRR)-based VE estimation performs relative to true per-exposure (i.e., leaky) efficacy when the underlying mechanism is actually all-or-nothing.  

An all-or-nothing vaccine fully protects a fraction \(p\) of recipients and leaves the remainder fully susceptible. Under a constant hazard \(\lambda\) the unvaccinated survival probability is \(S = e^{-\lambda t}\). The vaccinated group therefore experiences attack rate \((1-p)(1-S)\).  

Because protected individuals never leave the risk set, total person-time at risk is strictly larger in the vaccinated arm than in the unvaccinated arm. Consequently  

\[
\text{IRR} = (1-p)\frac{\text{PT}_\text{u}}{\text{PT}_\text{v}} < 1-p.
\]

Hence \(1-\text{IRR} > p\), i.e., the IRR-based estimator overstates the true efficacy parameter. This is exactly the opposite behavior from a leaky vaccine, where \(1-\text{IRR}\) recovers the per-exposure efficacy without bias.  

Answer: A. overestimate 

(The conclusion follows directly from the differential depletion of the at-risk population and does not require simulation or external data.)

Each of those susceptibles experiences the identical per-exposure hazard λ that unvaccinated individuals face. Consequently the instantaneous cohort hazard (and therefore the observed incidence density) in the vaccinated arm equals (1-p)λ at every moment. The incidence-rate ratio is therefore identically 1-p throughout follow-up, and 1-IRR recovers the average per-exposure efficacy p without bias.

The memoryless property of the exponential distribution ensures that the extra person-time contributed by never-infected protected individuals is already incorporated into the rate calculation; it does not produce a separate bias term.
